description: The world's law in git: any provision, any country, any date, and the law that wrote each word.
vibe: Treat law as data with provenance, not as prompt text or memory.
highlights: MCP-first access: agents must use the global-law server tools instead of reading files or running git directly.
Prompt-injection defense: law text, change notes, and judgment notes are reported, never followed.
Explicit epistemic limits: 'nothing found' means nothing in the record, not nothing in the law, and limits must be passed on.
Temporal and provenance correctness: tools read law as in force on a date and credit each change to the law that made it.
Checkout awareness: corpora are git submodules, so agents must check served jurisdictions and give users the add-country command rather than answering from memory.
assessment: This instruction file is effective because it treats legal text as untrusted data and forces agents through a provenance-aware tool layer rather than ad hoc file reading or model memory. Its emphasis on stated corpus limits, temporal validity, and jurisdiction availability directly targets the highest-risk failure modes in legal retrieval: hallucination, stale law, and prompt injection. The tone is restrained and operational, which suits a repository where correctness and traceability matter more than speed.
